title: The Great Migration and Harlem
objective: After this level you can explain why millions of Black Southerners moved north and how the Harlem Renaissance grew from it.
summary: About six million Black Southerners moved north and west to escape Jim Crow and find work, and in Harlem writers like Langston Hughes celebrated Black culture.

cards.headline: About six million Black Southerners packed up and moved north and west.
cards.body: It was one of the largest migrations in US history. Why did they go, and what did they build when they got there?

cards.headline: Pushed and pulled
cards.body: From the 1910s to the 1970s, migrants left the South to escape racial violence and the oppression of Jim Crow, and to find better jobs and schooling. World War I opened the door. From 1917, men leaving for the war and a drop in immigration from Europe left factory jobs that Black workers could now fill. Every train ticket north was a vote against Jim Crow.

cards.headline: New cities, old prejudice
cards.body: Migrants built new lives in cities such as New York, Chicago and Detroit. But the North had its own color line. Migrants met discrimination, including in housing, and racial violence in the Red Summer of 1919. Leaving the South didn't mean leaving racism behind.

cards.headline: Harlem's renaissance
cards.body: In New York's Harlem, the newcomers helped spark the Harlem Renaissance, which celebrated African American culture and achievement. Langston Hughes, whose first book of poems, The Weary Blues, appeared in 1926, became one of its leading writers. He said the people he met every day inspired his work, and blues and jazz gave it rhythm.

cards.headline: The Great Migration and Harlem: explained
